design_detail: Prospective community cohort (CARDIA: Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults), 5115 Black and White women and men aged 18 to 30 recruited in 1985 to 1986 in four US cities (Oakland, Chicago, Minneapolis, Birmingham) without selection for smoking, followed 20 years with spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20. Self-reported cannabis and tobacco smoking (current intensity at every exam; lifetime exposure in joint-years and pack-years) were modelled together in mixed linear models with individual age trajectories, first as four-level categories and then as flexible cubic splines. Tobacco was analysed in parallel as a positive control. Secondary analysis of a cohort designed for heart disease risk factors.
can_establish: How forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC) tracked with self-reported cannabis smoking, current and cumulative and mostly at light levels, in young adults over 20 years, with tobacco smoking modelled at the same time and shown to produce the expected dose-related loss.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis smoking causes or prevents any change in lung function (self-reported exposure, no measure of physical fitness, residual confounding possible); effects of heavy long-term smoking without tobacco (91 people had more than 10 joint-years and no tobacco, 40 more than 20); anything about respiratory symptoms, bronchitis, COPD, the FEV1-FVC ratio, lung volumes, gas transfer or emphysema (not reported or not measured); differences between joints, pipes and bongs (not recorded); effects of product strength or of vaping or eating.

sample.recruitment: Community sample from four US cities, recruited 1985 to 1986 to be balanced by race (Black, White), sex and age, not selected for smoking; healthy at enrolment; baseline plus 6 follow-up exams, 69% retention at year 20 (Methods › Study Design and Sample).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All visits with spirometry, smoking behaviour, second-hand smoke exposure, height and waist circumference. Of 20,777 visits with spirometry, 959 were excluded for incomplete smoking information, 114 for missing height or waist and 1 for an unknown date, leaving 19,703 visits (95%) from 5016 participants (98%).
sample.demographics: Mean age 25 (SD 4) at baseline; Black and White women and men were sampled in roughly equal numbers by design. 54% reported current cannabis or tobacco smoking, or both, at one or more exams. Black women were most likely to smoke tobacco only, White men cannabis only and Black men both. People who smoked cannabis tended to be taller and more active than people who did not smoke; people who smoked tobacco had lower education and income (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: 69% retention at year 20; attrition more common in people who smoked tobacco but not associated with cannabis use (Results, 1st paragraph). Mixed models use every available visit.
sample.selection_effects: Participants were Black and White adults from four cities, mostly people who smoked cannabis lightly (median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days); very heavy cumulative exposure is rare and mostly combined with tobacco, which limits estimates above about 10 joint-years. Attrition was more common in people who smoked tobacco.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at each exam. Cannabis: episodes in the last 30 days (current intensity) and lifetime joint-years (365 joints or pipe-fulls = 1 joint-year), built from baseline lifetime use, current intensity and a question on joints or pipe-fulls per episode, using assumptions given in an online appendix (not read). Tobacco: cigarettes per day and pack-years (1 pack-year = 7300 cigarettes); the authors cite a comparison with serum cotinine showing little misclassification of tobacco status.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cannabis exposure was mostly light: median 2 episodes (interquartile range 1 to 6) in the past 30 days in the cannabis-only group and 3 (1 to 9) in the group using both; median lifetime exposure 0.9 joint-years (0.2 to 2.8) and 1.5 (0.6 to 4.3). Tobacco medians 8 to 9 cigarettes a day and 7 to 9 pack-years. Route and method of smoking (joint, pipe, bong) were not recorded; strength and tobacco mixed into joints were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco was the main co-exposure and was modelled in the same model (current and lifetime, together with cannabis); the two exposures were strongly correlated. No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis was found for FEV1 or FVC. Other drugs and alcohol were not adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; current use was whatever the participant reported at each exam. The authors note that any acute widening of the airways after cannabis lasts about an hour and is unlikely to explain higher volumes unless many smoked just before testing.

comparison.controls: People with no reported exposure to the substance in question: the models compare each level of cannabis (or tobacco) exposure with zero, with tobacco and cannabis in the same model.
comparison.matching: No matching; covariate adjustment for year, centre and centre-by-year, race-sex group, education (a proxy for socio-economic status), baseline asthma, and flexible splines of age, height, waist circumference, second-hand smoke exposure (hours a week) and city-level particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Spirometry at year 0 gives a baseline for the cohort, but baseline use of cannabis by then was already present in some. Not among the adjustment variables: physical activity (the authors say people who smoked cannabis tended to be more active), income (Table 1 shows it differs by group), occupational exposures, other drug use and respiratory infections.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported or adjusted, apart from tobacco.

outcomes.instruments: Forced spirometry (FEV1 and FVC) with a Collins Survey 8-litre water-sealed spirometer and Eagle II Microprocessor at years 0, 2, 5 and 10, and an OMI rolling-seal spirometer at year 20 (average difference under 1% in a comparability test of 25 participants); standard quality control to published guidelines.
outcomes.validity_norms: Spirometry is a standard test; no comparison with predicted values is reported. The positive control (tobacco) shows the design can detect smoking-related loss.
outcomes.operationalization: Mean FEV1 and FVC differences in millilitres against zero exposure ('net association') and incremental differences per unit of exposure ('slope'), from models that follow each person's own age trajectory.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two outcomes against four smoking variables, in categories and in splines, with several slopes and net associations at chosen exposure levels; two-sided tests at 0.05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Four-level categories (Table 2), against zero exposure, all four smoking variables in one model: tobacco more than 20 cigarettes a day FEV1 -63 mL (95% CI -89 to -36), FVC -69 mL (-97 to -41); lifetime tobacco over 20 pack-years FEV1 -101 mL (-136 to -65). Cannabis only (current status) FEV1 +0.7 mL (-12 to 13), FVC +8.2 mL (-5 to 22). Lifetime cannabis 1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL (15 to 62), FVC +41 mL (14 to 67); 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL (32 to 100), FVC +54 mL (16 to 91); over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL (-6.5 to 79), FVC +59 mL (12 to 107). Current cannabis more than 20 episodes in 30 days FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1), FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49); P for trend across the four current-intensity categories 0.32 (FEV1) and 0.030 (FVC). Splines (Table 3): lifetime cannabis non-linear (P < 0.001 for both); slope at 2 joint-years FEV1 +13 mL per joint-year (6.4 to 20), FVC +20 (12 to 27); at 7 joint-years -0.4 (-2.6 to 1.8) and 0.0 (-2.4 to 2.5); at 20 and 50 joint-years FEV1 -2.2 (-4.6 to 0.3), P = 0.079, FVC +1.0 (-1.8 to 3.7). Net association at 7 joint-years FEV1 +53 mL (28 to 79), FVC +64 (36 to 92); at 20 joint-years FEV1 +27 (-10 to 64), FVC +76 (34 to 117); at 50 joint-years FEV1 -39 (-141 to 64), FVC +104 (-12 to 220). Current cannabis non-linear (P = 0.025 FEV1, 0.035 FVC); slope at 20 episodes a month FEV1 -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6), P = 0.017, FVC -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); no data at 40 episodes a month. Tobacco, linear: slope -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years; net FEV1 -332 mL (-401 to -263) and FVC -229 mL (-310 to -147) at 50 pack-years.
analysis.covariates: Year, centre, centre-by-year, race-sex group, education, baseline asthma, splines of age, height, waist circumference, second-hand smoke hours a week, PM10 and PM2.5, and interactions of age splines with race-sex, asthma, waist and height; random intercept and random 3-knot age spline per person, unstructured covariance; tobacco and cannabis, current and lifetime, in the same model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned. The authors state an a priori hypothesis that cannabis smoking should damage the airways like tobacco (Comment, 7th paragraph). Spline models were added to explore non-linear associations after the categorical models.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only FEV1 and FVC are reported; the FEV1-FVC ratio, the usual marker of airway obstruction, and respiratory symptoms are not, although the Comment discusses the ratio in earlier studies. The online appendix (assumptions for joint-years, spline details) was not read.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed. The authors state that the sample had too few people who smoked heavily to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use and that estimates at high exposure are imprecise (Comment, 1st and 8th paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a community cohort followed 20 years, tobacco smoking showed the expected linear loss of FEV1 and FVC (about 7 mL per pack-year), while cannabis smoking at the light levels typical of the cohort showed slightly higher FEV1 and FVC: at 7 joint-years net +53 mL (FEV1) and +64 mL (FVC). Above about 7 joint-years the cannabis curve levelled off for FEV1 and turned slightly down (slope -2.2 mL per joint-year, not significant), net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years were not significantly different from zero, and FVC stayed higher at 20 joint-years (and, not significantly, at 50). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes a month) showed a significant negative FEV1 slope (-3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017) with no significant net difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract conclusion: "Occasional and low cumulative marijuana use was not associated with adverse effects on pulmonary function." The final paragraph says the findings 'suggest an accelerated decline in pulmonary function with heavy use' and a need for caution. Gaps: (1) the final sentence is stronger than the results, since no net FEV1 difference at high exposure was significant and the authors themselves say the sample was too small to confirm harm; (2) the higher FEV1 and FVC at low exposure are explained by a speculative stretch or training effect without a test, and residual confounding by physical activity or fitness is not considered; (3) the abstract says the association 'leveled off or even reversed', which describes a curve whose reversal is not statistically significant; (4) the abstract opens by calling cannabis smoke very similar to tobacco smoke, which frames the question, but the data show a different pattern from tobacco.

timeline.event: Los Angeles cohort of people who smoked cannabis heavily and habitually (Tashkin et al., cited as ref 35; its title reports no accelerated FEV1 decline with age; the paper was not read here).
Dunedin birth cohort (Hancox et al., cited as ref 20): higher FVC and total lung capacity with cannabis exposure, as described in this paper's Comment.
This study: CARDIA, 20 years, cannabis and tobacco modelled together, non-linear association.

National Academies report describes this study as showing no adverse effect of occasional and low cumulative cannabis smoking on lung function and a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure, with few people at heavy exposure (committee's description)
Systematic review and meta-analysis that includes CARDIA (rated low risk of bias) among its studies of FEV1 and FVC and grades the lung-function evidence insufficient

replication.where_it_stands: The higher volumes and the absence of a clear FEV1 loss at light cumulative cannabis exposure fit the Dunedin cohort (higher FVC) and the Los Angeles cohort (no significant FEV1 fall), as the 2018 review describes them, whereas the Tucson cohort reported FEV1 reductions after one year; all rest on young, mostly light-exposure samples; the signal of a possible FEV1 loss at heavy exposure is single-study, not significant in net terms and from a sample with few people who smoked cannabis heavily without tobacco. CARDIA is also inside the pooled evidence of the 2018 review, so the two are not independent.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse (R01-DA-025067) funded this analysis; the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (N01-HC-95095, N01-HC-48047) funds CARDIA data collection and supports the committee that reviews all CARDIA publications. NIDA did not participate in CARDIA or review the manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: R. Kalhan: consultant for Boehringer-Ingelheim, Forest Laboratories and AstraZeneca; honoraria from GlaxoSmithKline, AstraZeneca, Quantia Communications and Medscape Education; industry-sponsored grants from GlaxoSmithKline and Boehringer-Ingelheim (respiratory-drug companies). S. Kertesz chaired a committee advising the Drug Treatment Task Force for the Chief Justice of Alabama and is employed by the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Otherwise none beyond federal funding.
funding.affiliations_note: No cannabis- or tobacco-industry funding or ties are declared. Author affiliations appear only as symbols in the extracted text.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort with many people who smoke cannabis heavily and no tobacco (for example more than 20 joint-years), recruited young and followed into their 40s and 50s with repeated spirometry including the FEV1-FVC ratio, plethysmography and gas transfer or low-dose CT, with physical activity, other drugs and the method and product of cannabis smoking recorded, and exposure checked against biomarkers.

domains.note: Extensive measured adjustment (race, sex, education, asthma, height, waist, second-hand smoke, particulate matter) and tobacco modelled at the same time, with tobacco as a positive control; but physical activity (which the authors say differs by cannabis use), income, other drug use and occupational dust were not adjusted, and tobacco and cannabis exposure were strongly correlated, so tobacco misclassification could leak into heavy-cannabis estimates.

Self-reported at each exam; lifetime joint-years built on assumptions in an appendix; no route, method, strength or tobacco-in-joints data; recall error acknowledged (the authors argue it is non-differential).
Community sample not selected for smoking; 98% of participants and 95% of visits had complete data.
No intervention after exposure is described that would differ by cannabis use.
69% retention at year 20; attrition associated with tobacco (included in the model) and not with cannabis; mixed models use all visits.

Standardised spirometry with quality control and a device comparison (under 1% difference); assessor blinding not reported; spirometry depends on effort, and recent cannabis smoking could widen the airways for about an hour.
No registered plan; spline analyses added to explore non-linearity; only FEV1 and FVC reported (not the FEV1-FVC ratio or symptoms); several exposure levels and slopes tested without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Some concerns rather than high because the design is strong for this question (20 years, repeated measures, individual age trajectories, tobacco modelled alongside as a positive control that behaves as expected), but physical activity and other co-exposures were not measured, cannabis exposure is self-reported and mostly light, and heavy cannabis-only exposure is rare. The study may be cited for the adjusted pattern of FEV1 and FVC against self-reported cannabis exposure at light and moderate cumulative levels in young adults, and for the parallel tobacco finding; not for a causal effect, for a benefit, for lung function after heavy long-term smoking or for any respiratory symptom or disease outcome.

key_findings.finding: 5115 adults aged 18 to 30 were recruited in 1985 to 1986 in four US cities; spirometry at years 0, 2, 5, 10 and 20 with 69% retention at year 20. Of 20,777 visits with spirometry, 19,703 (95%) from 5016 participants (98%) were used, 3.9 visits each on average; attrition was more common in people who smoked tobacco and not associated with cannabis use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Sample; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 54% reported current cannabis or tobacco smoking, or both, at one or more exams (neither 2305, tobacco only 851, cannabis only 795, both 1065). Cannabis exposure was nearly as common as tobacco but mostly light: median 2 to 3 episodes in the past 30 days against 8 to 9 cigarettes a day for tobacco; 91 participants had no tobacco exposure and more than 10 joint-years of cannabis (153 spirometry observations), 40 of them more than 20 joint-years (56 observations).

Tobacco (positive control): current smoking of more than 20 cigarettes a day was associated with FEV1 63 mL lower (95% CI -89 to -36) and FVC 69 mL lower (-97 to -41); lifetime exposure over 20 pack-years with FEV1 101 mL lower (-136 to -65). In spline models the association was linear and dose-related, with a slope of -7.0 mL per pack-year (-10 to -3.7) at 7 pack-years and net differences at 50 pack-years of -332 mL (-401 to -263) for FEV1 and -229 mL (-310 to -147) for FVC.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2; Table 3 (lifetime tobacco rows)

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, four-level categories, tobacco in the same model: lifetime exposure was associated with higher FVC and FEV1 than zero exposure (1 to 5 joint-years FEV1 +38 mL, 15 to 62; FVC +41 mL, 14 to 67; 6 to 10 joint-years FEV1 +66 mL, 32 to 100; FVC +54 mL, 16 to 91; over 10 joint-years FEV1 +36 mL, -6.5 to 79; FVC +59 mL, 12 to 107). Current heavy use (over 20 episodes in the past 30 days) was FEV1 -18 mL (-42 to 6.1) and FVC +20 mL (-5.2 to 49); people who used cannabis only differed little from people using neither (FEV1 +0.7 mL, -12 to 13; FVC +8.2 mL, -5 to 22), while tobacco only was -24 mL (-38 to -11) for FEV1.
key_findings.note: The Results text gives the lifetime category as 'more than 20' joint-years while Table 2 labels it 'more than 10'. P for trend across current-intensity categories 0.32 (FEV1) and 0.030 (FVC); across lifetime categories 0.049 and 0.013.

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, spline models: the association with lifetime exposure was non-linear (P < 0.001 for FEV1 and FVC). The slope was +13 mL per joint-year for FEV1 (6.4 to 20) and +20 mL for FVC (12 to 27) at 2 joint-years, about zero at 7 joint-years (FEV1 -0.4, -2.6 to 1.8; FVC 0.0, -2.4 to 2.5), and for FEV1 -2.2 mL per joint-year (-4.6 to 0.3, P = 0.079) at 20 and 50 joint-years. Net FEV1 difference against no exposure: +53 mL (28 to 79) at 7 joint-years, +27 mL (-10 to 64) at 20 and -39 mL (-141 to 64) at 50; net FVC +64 (36 to 92), +76 (34 to 117) and +104 (-12 to 220).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 3 (lifetime marijuana rows); Abstract (Results)
key_findings.note: The Results text gives the confidence interval of the -2.2 slope as -4.9 to 0.36 against -4.6 to 0.3 in the abstract and Table 3.

key_findings.finding: Current intensity, spline models: non-linear for both outcomes (FEV1 P = 0.025, FVC P = 0.035). At 20 episodes a month the FEV1 slope was -3.2 mL per episode a month (-5.8 to -0.6, P = 0.017) and the FVC slope -1.5 (-4.2 to 1.3); net differences at 20 episodes a month were FEV1 +14 mL (-4.7 to 32) and FVC +43 mL (23 to 63). No data at 40 episodes a month. The authors state the net FEV1 association became negative only at very high exposure (over 40 joint-years or 25 episodes a month) and not significantly.
No statistically significant interaction between tobacco and cannabis exposure was found for FEV1 or FVC.

The authors conclude that up to about 7 joint-years of lifetime exposure (for example 1 joint a day for 7 years or 1 joint a week for 49 years) gave no evidence that more exposure harms lung function, that at higher exposure the pattern levelled off or reversed especially for FEV1, and that the sample contained too few people with heavy use to confirm a harmful effect of very heavy use. They propose a stretch or training effect (one version called a speculative possibility) and a short-lived airway widening, which they consider unlikely to explain the higher volumes.

Limitations named by the authors: no plethysmography, diffusing capacity or imaging of emphysema; only a minority with very high cannabis exposure, fewer still without tobacco, so estimates at high exposure are imprecise; self-reported exposure with recall error and no record of smoking method; unmeasured confounding possible.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text gives the lifetime category with FVC +59 mL (12 to 107) and FEV1 +36 mL (-6.5 to 79) as 'more than 20 joint-years'; Table 2 labels it 'more than 10 joint-years' (the four lifetime categories are 0, 1 to 5, 6 to 10 and over 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use Table 2's definition (over 10 joint-years). The 2018 meta-analysis also cites it as over 10.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% interval of the FEV1 slope of -2.2 mL per joint-year is -4.9 to 0.36 in the Results text and -4.6 to 0.3 in the abstract and Table 3; the abstract says the slope applies 'at more than 10 joint-years' while Table 3 gives it at 20 and 50 joint-years (the slope at 7 joint-years is -0.4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the slope is not significant in either version (P = 0.079).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2, FEV1 for 11 to 20 pack-years of lifetime tobacco: the estimate -41 mL lies outside its printed interval (-38 to -14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in the tobacco rows; the surrounding rows and the spline results are consistent. Not used for the cannabis claim.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample counts differ between places: 19,703 visits from 5016 participants (Results), 19,704 observations (Table 2), 19,705 measurements from 5017 participants (Figure 1 legend). The 'Overall' FEV1 mean in Table 2 is printed as 3420 in a column headed liters while the rows are in liters.

The final paragraph says the findings 'suggest an accelerated decline in pulmonary function with heavy use', while the results show non-significant net FEV1 differences at 20 and 50 joint-years (+27 mL, -10 to 64; -39 mL, -141 to 64) and a non-significant spline slope (-2.2 mL per joint-year, P = 0.079). Only the slope for current use at 20 episodes a month was significant (-3.2 mL per episode a month, P = 0.017).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstatement in the discussion; the data allow 'possible' at most. Claims should cite the numbers, not that sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2018 meta-analysis reports the CARDIA FEV1 result '-18 mL' as current cannabis use with minimal exposure (2 to 3 episodes a month), and gives P = 0.32 and P = 0.03 for the FEV1 and FVC contrasts; in the primary paper -18 mL is the contrast for the heaviest current category (over 20 episodes in 30 days, 484 observations), 2 to 3 episodes a month is the median among people who smoked cannabis, and 0.32 and 0.030 are P values for trend across the four categories, not for that contrast (whose FVC interval -5.2 to 49 includes zero).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review understates the CARDIA exposure for this contrast and passes over the significant negative spline slope at 20 episodes a month; cite CARDIA from the primary paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3840897 (author manuscript; abstract, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1 to 3 as text, figure legends, comment, funding and conflict statements read; Figures 1 and 2 are images and were not extracted; the online appendix was not read)
